It then divided energy by duration to give an average power of 2,530 W; joules are energy and watts are power, so this is the average heating power over the 0.5-second interval.

On 2023-05-22, the assistant gave concrete’s specific heat capacity as approximately 880 J/(kg·°C), citing a KnowledgeBurrow webpage.

In the judgment excerpt shared by the user on 2023-05-26, the court considered Grounds 6 and 7 concerning the completion date under the owners’ and builder’s 2009 HIA contract. The Tribunal had found practical completion occurred on 20 October 2010, when the Final Occupation Certificate (FOC) was issued, reasoning that the builder was responsible for obtaining approvals and that the FOC formed part of the contractual building works.

The appeal court held that the Tribunal erred in interpreting the contract. The contract defined “building works” as physical works to be carried out, completed and handed over, including variations, and defined “practical completion” as completion of those works except for minor omissions or defects that do not prevent their reasonable use for their usual purpose. Although clause 7.1 made the builder responsible for obtaining and paying for building and planning approvals, that responsibility did not make the FOC part of the physical building works. The FOC was not necessary for practical completion of the building works themselves.

The appeal court concluded that the Tribunal erred in finding that the contractual completion date was 20 October 2010, when the FOC was issued. It therefore did not need to decide Ground 7, which challenged the finding as against the weight of evidence. The appeal was allowed in part; the Tribunal’s orders of 16 March 2020 were set aside; the matter was remitted to the Tribunal for rehearing; and the owners were ordered to pay the builder’s appeal costs.

The judgment excerpt also noted that the Tribunal treated the builder’s letter dated 19 July 2017, together with the builder’s correspondence, as part of a course of conduct supporting its finding that the parties had an agreement. The builder’s post-hearing submissions cited Haller rather than Butler v Fairclough; the Tribunal cited Haller at paragraph 20 of its Reasons, and the appeal court said the Tribunal was not required to give more detailed reasons.
